title: Halfway There
statement: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$, and let $h:S\to S$ be the function with $h(x)=1$ for $1\le x\le 4$ and $h(x)=5$ for $5\le x\le 8$. Find the number of functions $f:S\to S$ such that $f(f(x))=h(x)$ for every $x\in S$.
hints: The only values taken by $h$ are $1$ and $5$. Before counting anything, ask which values $f(1)$ and $f(5)$ can take.

Use substitution in the functional equation: write $f(f(f(x)))$ as $f$ applied to $f(f(x))$, and also as $f(f(\cdot))$ evaluated at $f(x)$. This shows that $f(h(x))=h(f(x))$, and putting $x=1$ and $x=5$ restricts $f(1)$ and $f(5)$.

The relation $f(h(x))=h(f(x))$ leaves two options: $f(1)=1,\ f(5)=5$ or $f(1)=5,\ f(5)=1$. It also shows that $f$ either preserves $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $\{5,6,7,8\}$ or interchanges them. In each option, choose which elements go straight to $1$ or $5$; every other element must map to a chosen element. With $0^0=1$, the counts are $\left(\sum_{j}\binom{3}{j}j^{3-j}\right)^2$ and $\sum_{p,q}\binom{3}{p}\binom{3}{q}q^{3-p}p^{3-q}$, with all indices running from $0$ to $3$. Now evaluate them and combine the results.
solution: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $B=\{5,6,7,8\}$. Since $f(h(x))=f^3(x)=h(f(x))$, we get $f(1)=h(f(1))\in\{1,5\}$ and $f(5)=h(f(5))\in\{1,5\}$. If $f(1)=1$ then $f(5)\ne1$, since otherwise $f(f(5))=1\ne5$, so $f(5)=5$. If $f(1)=5$ then $f(5)=f(f(1))=1$. Case 1: $f(1)=1,\ f(5)=5$. From $h(f(x))=f(h(x))$ we get $f(A)\subseteq A$ and $f(B)\subseteq B$. On $A$ the condition is $f(f(x))=1$. Let $J=\{x\in\{2,3,4\}:f(x)=1\}$ with $|J|=j$. Every other $x\in\{2,3,4\}$ must map into $J$, and any such map works. This gives $\sum_j\binom3j j^{3-j}=0+3+6+1=10$ choices, and likewise $10$ on $B$. Total $100$. Case 2: $f(1)=5,\ f(5)=1$. Similarly $f(A)\subseteq B$ and $f(B)\subseteq A$. Let $P=\{x\in\{2,3,4\}:f(x)=5\}$ and $Q=\{x\in\{6,7,8\}:f(x)=1\}$, with sizes $p,q$. Then $\{2,3,4\}\setminus P$ must map into $Q$ and $\{6,7,8\}\setminus Q$ into $P$, and any such maps work, since then $f(f(x))=1$ on $A$ and $5$ on $B$. The count is $$\sum_{p,q}\binom3p\binom3q q^{3-p}p^{3-q}.$$ The terms are $27$ for $(0,3)$ and $(3,0)$, $9$ for $(1,1)$, $36$ for $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$, $27$ for $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$, $36$ for $(2,2)$, $9$ for $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$, and $1$ for $(3,3)$. All other terms vanish. The sum is $54+9+72+54+36+18+1=244$. Total: $100+244=344$.
